title: Unescaped quotes in onclick strings took the whole app down
symptom: On the deployed site no tab rendered and every nav click was dead. The page looked fine; nothing worked.
root_cause: Five onclick handlers were built as JS strings containing unescaped single quotes inside single-quoted string literals. That is a parse error, and a parse error anywhere in an inline script kills the entire script, not the one handler.
detection: Reported from the live site after deploy.
fix: Escape the quotes, and make the build parse every inline script with node before it will write a page.
guard: build.py node-parses every inline script and fails the build on a syntax error
lesson: Generated code is code. If your build writes JavaScript into a string, the build must parse the result, because the blast radius of one bad character is the whole file, not the line.
cost: a live outage of the trainer

title: School URLs vanished from the sitemap when the data file was split
symptom: Per-school pages were live and correct, and absent from sitemap.xml.
root_cause: The sitemap generator read schools.json. When the library was split into one file per school, nothing read the new directory, and a loop over an empty list emits nothing rather than failing.
detection: Noticed while reviewing the built sitemap.
fix: Generate sitemap entries from the same directory scan the pages are built from.
guard: the build asserts the sitemap URL count matches the page count
lesson: A refactor that moves data has to be followed to every reader, and a loop over nothing is the quietest failure in programming. Derive counts from one source and assert they agree.
cost: unknown period of missing indexation

title: Item banks were different on every build because Python randomises hash()
symptom: Two builds of the same commit produced different banks, and the per-section bias figures pinned in the test file drifted run to run.
root_cause: build_banks.py seeded each category with abs(hash(exam + skill)). Python randomises string hashing per process by default.
detection: A pinned test figure would not stay pinned.
fix: Seed from zlib.crc32, which is stable across processes.
guard: three consecutive builds must produce identical output
lesson: Any generator that claims reproducibility must be seeded from something stable across processes. hash() is not, in Python, and the failure shows up as a flaky test rather than as a wrong answer.
cost: a flaky ratchet that would have been disabled eventually

title: A shadowed variable silently deleted 3000 items
symptom: ACT Maths dropped from 4500 items to 1500 and the build reported success.
root_cause: Adding an ACT English mapping declared a second ACT_MAP that shadowed the existing one. Nothing errors when a map is smaller than it used to be.
detection: Comparing the reported category counts against the previous build.
fix: Merge the maps properly and read the section per skill.
guard: the build prints per-category counts and the test file pins them
lesson: Deletion by shadowing is invisible. Any collection whose size is a fact about the product needs its size asserted, not just its contents.
cost: 3000 items, caught before merge

title: The adaptive engine was learning from nobody
symptom: The attempts table held zero rows in production while the app was plainly being used.
root_cause: Cloud.logAttempt returns early without a signed-in user, and the product deliberately requires no account. So the one path that recorded answers was the one path most users never took.
detection: Querying the production table and finding it empty.
fix: item_events: an unlinkable telemetry table with no user, session, device or address column, which is exactly why it needs no consent gate.
guard: smoke_consent asserts the telemetry body carries no identifying field
lesson: Check that your instrumentation fired at all before you trust anything built on it. An empty table looks identical to a quiet week.
cost: weeks of telemetry never recorded

title: Sentence equivalence items were unanswerable however well you answered
symptom: Every GRE sentence equivalence item graded as wrong.
root_cause: The items carry a two-element key and the engine graded by requiring an array of two, but answerInputs had no branch for that type, so they rendered as single pick and returned a scalar.
detection: Rendering and grading one item of every schema.
fix: Add the missing input branch.
guard: smoke_items renders and grades one item from all 182 generator schemas at phone width
lesson: A type system spread across a renderer and a grader will drift. The cheapest guard is one that exercises every variant end to end, once.
cost: eleven items unusable since they shipped

title: The dedup key counted a reshuffled question as a new one
symptom: Bank counts were inflated. The same question with its options rearranged looked distinct.
root_cause: canon() hashed the choices in the order they appeared, while the answer's position is randomised per draw.
detection: Sorting the choices before hashing, which immediately collapsed the counts.
fix: Sort the choices inside canon().
guard: canon() sorts, and the build reports distinct counts per category
lesson: A deduplication key must be canonical under every transformation the item legitimately undergoes. Ask what varies per draw before you hash.
cost: four ACT categories reported far above their real size

title: Four passages produced five hundred fake distinct questions
symptom: A reading generator with four passages reported five hundred distinct stated-idea items.
root_cause: The identity of a reading item is the passage plus the question asked, not the choices offered. The same stem with the same key varied only in which distractors came along.
detection: Reading the generated output rather than its count.
fix: canon() lets a generator declare that its identity is the passage plus the question.
guard: per-category distinct counts printed at build time
lesson: The same inflation arrives through a different door every time you close one. When you fix a dedup bug, ask what else shares an identity.
cost: would have shipped a bank five hundred deep and four questions wide

title: Two conditionals hashed identically and half the inference items would have vanished
symptom: Half of a passage's inference questions disappeared from the corpus.
root_cause: Both conditionals produced the stem 'which of the following can be properly inferred from the passage', so they hashed to the same value and one was dropped as a duplicate.
detection: Measuring true yield per passage.
fix: Each conditional names the case it asks about.
guard: yield per passage is measured and recorded, not assumed
lesson: Dedup can be wrong in both directions. An over-broad key deletes real content as silently as a narrow one inflates it.
cost: half the inference items in any corpus

title: CSS comments do not nest, and one placeholder killed the palette on 1451 pages
symptom: The colour palette was gone from every college page. It looked like a design problem and was chased as one for hours.
root_cause: A `{{CHROME_CSS}}` placeholder was left inside an opening CSS comment in rankings_base.css. The first */ closes the outer comment, so everything after it was live CSS that overwrote the palette.
detection: Eventually, by reading the built CSS rather than the template.
fix: Remove the nested comment.
lesson: CSS comments do not nest. When a whole page category loses its styling, read the built artefact, not the source that produced it.
cost: hours, on 1451 pages

title: A length guard silently dropped sixteen valid items
symptom: Sixteen items never appeared in the bank.
root_cause: The guard measured characters, and the items were legitimately longer than the limit in characters while being normal in content.
detection: Counting inputs against outputs.
fix: Measure what the guard actually cares about.
guard: input and output counts are compared at every filter stage
lesson: Every filter needs its rejection count reported. A filter that silently drops is indistinguishable from an input that was never there.
cost: sixteen items

title: Postgres fired triggers alphabetically and revoked every adult opt-in
symptom: Legitimate adult opt-ins to the data sharing programme were silently revoked.
root_cause: Postgres fires same-timing triggers in alphabetical order by name. profiles_sharing_eligibility sorted before profiles_sync_age_tier, so eligibility was judged against a stale age tier.
detection: Testing the guarantee the triggers were supposed to provide, rather than reading the trigger code.
fix: Numeric prefixes on trigger names to force the order.
guard: src/sql smoke tests assert the guarantee, not the implementation
lesson: Postgres fires same-timing triggers alphabetically. If two triggers on one table have an order dependency, encode it in the name, and test the outcome rather than the code.
cost: every adult opt-in, silently

title: UPDATE OF fires on the columns named in the statement, not the ones that changed
symptom: Updating birth_year stored a minor's tier and skipped the eligibility check entirely.
root_cause: UPDATE OF <columns> keys off the columns named in the UPDATE statement, not off what actually changed and not off what an earlier BEFORE trigger wrote into NEW.
detection: Same guarantee test as INC-0012.
fix: Fire on every update and compare OLD to NEW inside the function.
guard: sharing eligibility fires on every update
lesson: UPDATE OF is a statement-shape filter, not a change filter. If you need 'when this value changed', compare OLD and NEW yourself.
cost: a minor could pass the adult gate

title: A hardcoded count in the meta description went stale, and Google showed it
symptom: The meta description claimed 1,451 colleges after the number changed. og:description and twitter:description both derive from that tag, so all three were wrong.
root_cause: A figure typed into a template instead of computed at build time, which is the exact failure build-time counting exists to prevent.
detection: Reading the built page.
fix: Derive the number from the same count the pages are built from.
guard: no hardcoded corpus counts in templates
lesson: Any number in user-facing copy that describes the size of something must be computed from that thing at build time. The moment it is typed, it has a half-life.
cost: a wrong figure in the search result snippet

title: The whole bank blocked first paint: 20 seconds to the first question on 3G
symptom: On throttled regular 3G, 20.3 seconds to the first GMAT question and 23.4 for ACT.
root_cause: The entire item bank shipped as a blocking script. It grew past ten megabytes without anyone measuring what that cost.
detection: A throttled measurement, added because the number had never been taken.
fix: A strided starter bank plus an async remainder that pushes into the same array. ACT 7.6s, GMAT 11.0s; blocking download 11.3MB to 1.2MB.
guard: smoke_load measures time to first question under throttling
lesson: Nobody notices a page getting slower one commit at a time. Put the number in a test the first time you care about it, not the first time somebody complains.
cost: every visitor on a slow connection, for weeks

title: The performance test waited for the load event, which waits for the thing being optimised
symptom: A change that made the page usable nine times faster would have reported no improvement.
root_cause: smoke_load waited for the load event. The load event waits for the async bank, which is precisely the part the fix moved off the critical path.
detection: The number refused to move when it obviously should have.
fix: Wait for the first question to be answerable.
guard: smoke_load waits on the user-visible milestone
lesson: Measure the moment the user can act, not a browser lifecycle event. A test that measures the wrong instant is worse than no test, because it produces a number people trust.
cost: would have hidden the entire win

title: A build guard silently narrowed its own scope when the counts grew
symptom: The item-count guard kept passing while checking nothing.
root_cause: The guard matched \d{2,4}. When the banks passed ten thousand, the two largest counts stopped matching the pattern and fell out of the check.
detection: Reading the guard while raising the counts.
fix: Match any run of digits.
guard: the guard asserts how many counts it checked
lesson: A regex with a length bound is a guard with an expiry date. Assert the number of things checked, not only that the checks passed.
cost: the two largest banks unchecked

title: The Do Not Sell button was invisible from the day it shipped
symptom: White text on a transparent background on a white page. A legally required control that nobody could see.
root_cause: The page referenced nine colour custom properties that exist nowhere. CSS does not treat an undefined custom property as an error; it falls back to the initial value and paints.
detection: An automated contrast audit across every page.
fix: Define the tokens and fix seven contrast failures, all site wide because all lived in shared chrome.
guard: weekly_audit checks computed contrast on every page
lesson: An undefined CSS custom property is silent. Audit computed colour, not authored colour, and do it on the rendered page.
cost: an invisible compliance control for the life of the page
recurs_why: INC-0050 lesson: the same undefined-property failure will find you repeatedly, at every severity from one icon to an invisible legal control

title: The audit reported a working link as broken
symptom: A false positive in the launch audit.
root_cause: Relative link resolution in the audit did not match the browser's.
detection: Checking a reported failure by hand.
fix: Resolve links the way the browser does.
lesson: Check your checker. A tool that cries wolf gets muted, and then it is worse than nothing.
cost: trust in the audit

title: Revoking EXECUTE from anon did nothing while PUBLIC still held it
symptom: Functions stayed callable after their grants were revoked from anon and authenticated.
root_cause: PUBLIC is a separate grantee. A leading =X/postgres in pg_proc.proacl means PUBLIC holds EXECUTE, and revoking from the named roles changes nothing.
detection: Re-running the Supabase advisors instead of trusting the per-role grants.
fix: Revoke from PUBLIC as well, everywhere.
guard: every migration revokes from public, anon, authenticated together
lesson: In Postgres, revoking from every role you can name still leaves PUBLIC. Verify with the advisors or by reading the acl, never by reading your own migration.
cost: an open function surface believed closed

title: A test passed because nothing was configured at all
symptom: smoke_funnel's 'nothing sent on refusal' assertion passed. It would have passed with the feature deleted.
root_cause: The test used storage key sfn_consent instead of sfn_consent_v1, so consent was never set up, so nothing was ever sent, so the assertion held vacuously.
detection: Fixing the key, which immediately exposed a real bug underneath.
fix: Use the real key, and assert the positive case as well as the negative.
guard: every 'nothing happens' assertion is paired with a 'something happens' assertion
lesson: A negative assertion passes when the system is broken in the right way. Always pair it with the positive case, or it is testing nothing.
cost: a real bug hidden behind a green check

title: A try/catch caught nothing because the call inside it does not throw
symptom: An error path never ran.
root_cause: The wrapped call signals failure by return value, not by throwing, so the catch was unreachable.
detection: A review bot playing a full exam against the real engine.
fix: Check the return value.
guard: review_bot.js sits each exam repeatedly against the real engine
lesson: try/catch around an API that returns errors is decoration. Know which convention each call uses before you wrap it.
cost: a silent failure path

title: www and the apex were two origins, so consent and rankings split in half
symptom: Two hostnames served the same site. localStorage is per origin, so a visitor who arrived on both had two consent states and their ranking signal was split.
root_cause: No canonical host redirect. The Cloudflare connector available here has no zone-level tools, so it had to be solved in the Worker.
detection: Reasoning about origin scoping while investigating traffic.
fix: src/worker.mjs 301s www to the apex, with run_worker_first true so the asset router does not answer first.
guard: smoke_redirect asserts the redirect and that run_worker_first stays true
lesson: Two hostnames are two origins and therefore two of everything the browser scopes by origin. Pick one and redirect on the server, not in a meta tag.
cost: split consent state and diluted ranking signal

title: The .git directory was being served on production
symptom: https://startfromnowhere.com/.git/config returned 200.
root_cause: .assetsignore excluded src/, data/ and supabase/ but not **/.git. Cloudflare's asset uploader walks the repository root, which is the assets directory.
detection: An adversarial review of the deploy exclusion list, after the first version of that list had already shipped.
fix: Exclude **/.git, and rewrite the guard to derive what must be served from real references rather than a hand-written allowlist.
guard: smoke_redirect derives the must-serve set with git check-ignore and asserts the source is excluded
lesson: An exclusion list is a denylist, and denylists are wrong by omission. Derive the allowed set from what the built pages actually reference.
cost: the full repository history publicly readable

title: A stale edge cache made a fixed 404 look like a live 200
symptom: After the fix deployed, /.git/config still returned 200.
root_cause: Cloudflare had cached the response with max-age=300. The fix was live; the verification was reading the cache.
detection: Re-requesting with a cache-busting query string, which returned 404.
fix: None needed in code.
lesson: Verify a cache-fronted fix with a cache-busting request, or you are testing the cache. This costs one query parameter and saves an hour of chasing a fix that already worked.
cost: minutes, and nearly a wrong conclusion

title: I reported a regression that was seed noise
symptom: I reported that SAT band coverage fell from 88 to 72 percent after an engine change.
root_cause: I compared a single seed before and after. Across seeds 3, 7 and 11 the baseline was 52, 88 and 80 against 72, 80 and 72 for the change. The spread between seeds was larger than the effect.
detection: Running more seeds because the number looked too clean.
fix: Report across seeds, never one.
guard: review_bot runs multiple seeds and reports the spread
lesson: A stochastic measurement on one seed is an anecdote. If your system has randomness, a single-run before-and-after cannot distinguish a change from the weather.
cost: a false regression report, corrected in the same session

title: A 29.88 MiB bank file would have failed the deploy the moment it merged
symptom: None yet. The build succeeded locally and the deploy would have rejected the file.
root_cause: Cloudflare Workers static assets cap a single file at 25 MiB. Raising the generated banks pushed the ACT rest-bank past it.
detection: Checking the platform limit against the real output size before pushing.
fix: Chunk the rest-bank at 18 MiB per file and glob the chunks in numeric order.
guard: the build fails on any asset over 25 MiB
lesson: Know your platform's hard limits and assert them in the build. A deploy-time rejection is a bad place to learn a number your build could have told you.
cost: would have broken the deploy

title: The service worker precache regex did not match the chunked files
symptom: Chunked bank files would not have been precached offline.
root_cause: The IMMUTABLE pattern was /bank_rest\.js$/, which does not match bank_rest1.js.
detection: Reading the service worker while changing the file naming.
fix: /bank_rest\d*\.js$/.
guard: smoke_offline asserts every bank chunk is precached
lesson: When you change a filename scheme, grep for the old name as a string, including inside regexes. A pattern is a hardcoded name wearing a disguise.
cost: offline would have silently degraded

title: A sequential colour ramp inverts direction between themes, and the label text did not
symptom: White heatmap labels on a light cell in dark mode.
root_cause: A sequential ramp runs light to dark in a light theme and dark to light in a dark theme. The label colour was hardcoded white, so it was correct in one theme and unreadable in the other.
detection: Rendering the chart in dark mode and looking at it.
fix: An --sfnc-on-seq token that flips with the theme.
guard: smoke_charts asserts token parity between the light and dark blocks
lesson: A dark mode does not break by having a wrong colour. It breaks by missing one. Any colour paired with a ramp has to move with the ramp.
cost: an unreadable chart in one theme

title: The theme parity test matched by name prefix and caught a font size
symptom: The parity guard flagged --text-xs, which is a length, not a colour.
root_cause: Token selection was by name prefix rather than by whether the value is a colour.
detection: Reading the failure.
fix: Select tokens by inspecting the value.
guard: smoke_charts selects by value, not name
lesson: Classify by what a thing is, not by what it is called. Naming conventions are a hint, never a type.
cost: a false failure

title: The browser suites had never actually run, because npm install had not
symptom: Browser tests appeared to be part of the suite and were not being executed.
root_cause: playwright was listed as a devDependency and node_modules did not exist in the environment.
detection: Running them by hand and getting a module-not-found.
fix: Add npm install and playwright install to CI, and check in package.json.
guard: CI runs npm run test:browser
lesson: A test that is not wired into CI is a test that does not exist. Prove a suite runs in the place it is supposed to run, not on your machine.
cost: an unknown number of regressions unnoticed

title: ARR was rounded to whole dollars and lost real money at small scale
symptom: $159.84 of ARR printed as $160.
root_cause: The currency formatter was called with zero decimal places for the larger tiles, a rule chosen for readability at scale and applied at a scale where cents still matter.
detection: A smoke test whose expected values were computed by hand before the page was written.
fix: Keep cents below a thousand dollars, drop them above.
guard: smoke_business asserts the exact printed figures
lesson: A fixed rounding rule is wrong at one end of the range or the other. Pick the precision from the magnitude, and write the expected number down before you write the code that produces it.
cost: a wrong figure on the tile the owner reads most closely

title: The dashboard test measured a hidden element and passed
symptom: Layout and contrast assertions passed on a view that was never displayed.
root_cause: The admin view carries a hidden class. A display:none element still answers innerText and getComputedStyle, so every assertion held on a box that had never been laid out.
detection: Screenshotting the result and seeing the dashboard was not in it.
fix: Call show('admin') and dismiss the onboarding overlay before measuring.
guard: smoke_business asserts the view is on screen and taller than 400px before measuring it
lesson: Before you measure a layout, assert the thing is rendered. Hidden elements answer most DOM questions, and they answer them wrongly.
cost: a layout suite that tested nothing, caught the same day

title: A line chart interpolated between discrete money events
symptom: A line drawn between $13.32 on the 18th and $4.99 on the 19th, passing through every value in between.
root_cause: Money movement was charted as a time series. A line encodes continuity, and these are discrete events on particular days.
detection: Rendering it and looking at it.
fix: Bars for movement and cash. Lines are reserved for measures that genuinely vary continuously.
lesson: Chart form is a claim about the data. A line claims the values in between existed. Ask whether that claim is true before choosing it.
cost: a chart that implied numbers that never happened

title: Two Stripe event types announce one new subscription
symptom: None: caught in design. Logging new subscriptions from both checkout.session.completed and customer.subscription.created would have doubled new MRR.
root_cause: Stripe announces a new subscription through both events, with different event ids, in no guaranteed order.
detection: Working out the idempotency key before writing the handler.
fix: A partial unique index on (source, subscription_id, kind) for the once-per-lifetime kinds, so the database decides rather than whichever event arrived first.
guard: billing_events_once_idx
lesson: Idempotency belongs in the database, not in the handler. Handlers race; unique indexes do not.
cost: would have doubled the headline revenue figure

title: charge.amount_refunded is cumulative, so partial refunds double-count
symptom: None: caught in design. A second partial refund reports the running total, which would have counted the first refund twice.
root_cause: Stripe's charge object reports total refunded to date, not the amount of this refund.
detection: Reading the field's semantics rather than its name.
fix: Use the most recent entry in the refunds list, falling back to the cumulative total for the ordinary single full refund.
lesson: Read what a payment field means, not what it is called. Cumulative and incremental fields look identical until the second event.
cost: would have overstated refunds

title: Cancellation erases the number you need to record the cancellation
symptom: None: caught in design. Churned MRR would always have been zero.
root_cause: The profile write on cancellation nulls plan_amount_cents and plan_interval. That row was the only place the departing subscriber's price still existed.
detection: Tracing the order of writes in the handler.
fix: Read the prior profile state before the cancellation write, and log what they were paying.
guard: priorState() is called before writeProfile in both the deleted and updated branches
lesson: When a write is destructive, capture what you need from the old value first. Ask what question you will want to answer after this row is gone.
cost: would have reported zero churn forever

title: One exam's progress blob overwrote another's
symptom: None shipped: caught before release. A student practising two exams would have had one exam's progress destroyed by the other.
root_cause: Progress was stored under a single key. Making the engine multi-exam added a second writer to the same slot without keying the slot by exam.
detection: Reviewing the cross-exam data paths while adding the second exam.
fix: Key the stored state per exam.
guard: engine tests run once per exam and assert progress isolation
lesson: The moment a single-tenant store becomes multi-tenant, every key in it is a collision waiting to happen. Enumerate the writers before you add the second tenant, not after.
cost: would have destroyed real progress

title: 225 of 302 correct answers sat at position A
symptom: Three quarters of the correct answers in a new bank were the first option.
root_cause: Items were authored with the key written first and the position never randomised.
detection: Counting the key positions, a check nobody had run.
fix: Randomise the key position per draw.
guard: the test suite pins the key-position distribution
lesson: In any set of multiple-choice content, count where the answers are. A positional tell makes the whole set worthless to a test-wise user, and it is invisible item by item.
cost: a bank that could be beaten without reading it

title: The easier module was not easier
symptom: An adaptive test routed weaker students to a second module that was supposed to be easier, and was not.
root_cause: The two modules were assembled without comparing their difficulty distributions.
detection: Measuring the mean difficulty of each module.
fix: Assemble the modules against a difficulty target and assert it.
guard: module difficulty is asserted at build time
lesson: If your system branches on difficulty, measure that the branches actually differ. A label is not a property.
cost: adaptive routing that did nothing

title: A signed-in user could grant themselves a paid plan
symptom: The plan column was writable by the authenticated role, so any signed-in browser session could set its own plan to the top tier.
root_cause: Column-level grants on the profiles table included the billing columns. Row Level Security controls which rows you can touch, not which columns.
detection: Auditing the grants rather than the policies.
fix: Remove the billing columns from the grants entirely. Only the service role, used by the webhook, can write them.
guard: the billing columns are absent from the column grants
lesson: Row Level Security is row-level. Which columns a role may write is a separate grant, and anything money depends on belongs to the service role alone.
cost: free access to every paid tier

title: Every trialing subscriber would have been left on the free plan
symptom: A checkout that starts a free trial did not upgrade the account.
root_cause: The handler checked for a payment status of paid. A session that starts a trial settles as no payment required, which is not paid.
detection: Reading the processor's status vocabulary rather than assuming it.
fix: Accept both settled states.
guard: smoke_billing covers the trial path in both auth states
lesson: Enumerate every value a third-party status field can take before you branch on one of them. The value you did not think of is usually the one that matters commercially.
cost: every trial would have failed to grant access

title: The GRE app told GRE students to calibrate at the wrong test maker's site
symptom: A shipped application displayed a score card headed with a different exam's name and linked students to that exam's official site.
root_cause: The template forked on the exam id in seven places and treated not-SAT as the original exam. Adding a third exam made every one of those branches wrong.
detection: Reading the built page for the third exam.
fix: Per-exam copy moved into the registry and resolved from the injected exam id.
guard: a headless check asserts each app names itself
lesson: A conditional that treats not-A as the original case is a bug the day a third case exists. Resolve variants from data, and the third one costs a row rather than a search.
cost: a live app misidentifying itself

title: The longest option was the correct answer 81 percent of the time
symptom: A student who picked the longest option without reading the question scored 81 percent against a chance level of 20.
root_cause: Distractors were shorter than keys because a correct answer is naturally more qualified, and nothing measured the resulting length distribution.
detection: Measuring the accuracy of a strategy that ignores the question entirely.
fix: About ninety items had distractors rewritten to carry comparable development, each added clause chosen to leave the option wrong for the reason it was already wrong. 81 percent to 38, then to chance in a later pass.
guard: a ratchet pins the length tell and fails if it rises
lesson: Test your content against the strategies a lazy adversary would use, not only against whether it is correct. Measure the score of a rule that ignores the question.
cost: a section that could be beaten without reading it

title: The error reporter reported its own failures, in a loop
symptom: 267 rows in the error table, one per page a crawler swept.
root_cause: fetch rejects on a network error, it does not throw, so the try/catch around the reporting call caught nothing. The rejected promise reached the unhandledrejection handler, which called the reporter again. The analytics beacon had the identical trap.
detection: Reading the error table and noticing the shape of the rows.
fix: Handle the rejection, and never report from inside the reporter.
lesson: Anything that reports failures must not be able to report its own. Check whether each call rejects or throws before you wrap it, and make the reporting path unable to re-enter itself.
cost: 267 junk rows and a self-sustaining loop

title: The error queue was 81 percent other people's blocked scripts
symptom: 1,202 of the first 1,490 rows in the error table were one third-party beacon being blocked by ad blockers.
root_cause: The handler captured every error on the page, including ones from scripts the site does not control and cannot fix.
detection: Clustering the rows and looking at the largest cluster.
fix: Filter third-party script errors, and give the triage queue a permanent noise label.
guard: the triage queue mutes a cluster marked noise
lesson: An error feed with no filter is a feed nobody reads. Signal has to be defended, and the cheapest defence is a human label that mutes permanently, so the queue gets quieter as it learns.
cost: a monitoring surface that was 81 percent noise

title: Excluding the design directory would have shipped the legal pages with no styling
symptom: None: caught in draft. Terms and Privacy would have rendered with no font, no colour and no background.
root_cause: Those two pages load a stylesheet from the design directory that is nothing but imports of the token files. Excluding the directory from the deploy removed both the stylesheet and the tokens it imports.
detection: An adversarial re-read of the exclusion list against what the built pages actually reference.
fix: Re-include the tokens and the stylesheet, and rewrite the guard to read every href and src out of the built pages and follow one level of CSS import, instead of comparing against a list kept by hand.
guard: smoke_redirect derives the must-serve set from the built pages
lesson: A guard that is a hand-kept list of safe paths is written by the same hand that made the mistake. Derive the safe set from the artefact, not from memory.
cost: two legal pages unstyled, caught before deploy

title: Error recovery in the CSS parser swallowed the palette silently
symptom: Score bars rendered as empty gaps and panels lost their borders on 1,451 college pages and the rankings.
root_cause: A nested comment ended early, the leftover words became a selector, and the CSS parser's error recovery discarded the :root colour block that followed it. Every grey and navy variable on those pages resolved to nothing. There is no error anywhere in this chain; CSS is specified to recover and continue.
detection: The missing borders eventually gave it away, after the missing colours did not.
fix: Remove the nested comment.
guard: weekly_audit checks computed colour on every page
lesson: CSS never fails loudly. A malformed rule is skipped, a bad selector eats the block after it, and an undefined variable paints as nothing. Anything that matters visually has to be asserted on the rendered page, because the parser will not tell you.
cost: the palette on over 1,450 pages

title: Two pages told the same story with different numbers after a reweighting
symptom: The rankings index still showed figures from before a scoring change while the methodology page showed the new ones.
root_cause: Two artefacts derived from one model, and only one was regenerated.
detection: Reading both pages after the change.
fix: Derive both from the same computed values at build time.
guard: both figures are printed by the build from one source
lesson: When one model feeds two pages, generate both from the model in the same pass. Two places that must agree will not, and the reader who notices is the reader you were trying to convince.
cost: a visible contradiction between two pages

title: A landing-page icon referenced a colour token that did not exist
symptom: One game icon on the landing grid rendered without its colour.
root_cause: An undefined custom property, which CSS treats as a fallback rather than an error.
detection: Looking at the page on a phone during a mobile pass.
fix: Use a defined token.
guard: weekly_audit checks computed colour on every page
lesson: The same undefined-property failure will find you repeatedly, at every severity from one icon to an invisible legal control. One audit of computed colour catches the whole class.
cost: one icon, and the same root cause later cost a compliance control

title: Fixing repeats directly left a side door through passage groups
symptom: After a freshness gate cut avoidable repeats from 276 to 9 on one exam, one exam still served 117 and another 941 across 25 sittings.
root_cause: The gate picked an unserved anchor item, and then the group expansion pulled in every question sharing that passage, including the ones already answered. The gate was applied to the anchor and not to what the anchor dragged with it.
detection: A review bot counting avoidable repeats across 25 sittings per exam.
fix: The group keeps the anchor and any unseen sibling and drops the rest, so a group can never come back empty.
guard: the review bot counts avoidable repeats and the number is pinned
lesson: When you add a filter, find every path that adds items after the filter runs. A gate on the entry point is not a gate on the set.
cost: repeats persisting on two exams after the fix was believed complete

title: Two games signalled right and wrong by colour alone
symptom: Outcomes in two timed games were distinguishable only by colour, and nothing was announced.
root_cause: The games were built for speed and the feedback was styling rather than content.
detection: An accessibility pass over the games.
fix: Announce outcomes in a live region, and give a flipped tile a spoken identity. Colour is now secondary to a word in both.
guard: smoke tests assert the live region announces outcomes
lesson: Never encode a state by colour alone. The word also survives greyscale printing, forced-colors mode and a glance from across a room, so it is better for everyone and not only for the people it is required by.
cost: two games unusable with a screen reader

title: The playbook's own citation guard failed CI on its first run
symptom: CI reported all 37 cited commits as nonexistent, with 'fatal: Not a valid object name' for every one.
root_cause: The checkout action shallow-clones by default, so no historical commit is present in the CI working copy. The guard was correct and its environment assumption was not.
detection: The first CI run of the guard.
fix: fetch-depth: 0 on the checkout so the history is actually there to check.
guard: fetch-depth: 0 in the workflow
lesson: A guard that reads the repository needs the repository. CI checkouts are shallow by default, and anything that walks history, blames a line or resolves an old hash will fail in a way that looks like the data is wrong rather than the clone.
cost: one red CI run

title: The first fix asked the wrong question and muted a working check
symptom: After guarding on 'is this a shallow clone', the citation check stopped running locally, where it had been working perfectly and verifying all 52 citations.
root_cause: This clone is shallow and still holds every commit the ledger cites, which is the normal case. Shallowness does not imply missing history, so the guard disabled itself in the one environment where it was useful.
detection: Reading the output after the fix and noticing a check had turned into a skip.
fix: Ask whether ANY citation resolved. None at all means the history is absent; some means those particular citations are wrong.
guard: the check degrades only when zero citations resolve
lesson: When you add a condition that skips a check, make sure it describes the failure and not something merely correlated with it. A skip is indistinguishable from a pass in the output, so the fix for a noisy check can silently delete it.
cost: a working check disabled for the length of one edit

title: A new browser suite hardcoded this machine's browser directory and crashed in CI
symptom: ENOENT scandir /opt/pw-browsers on the first CI run of the dashboard suite, after every other suite had passed.
root_cause: The suite read a browser directory that exists in the development sandbox and not on a CI runner, where Playwright installs browsers in its own location. The older suites pass process.env.CHROMIUM_PATH straight through, which is undefined in CI and correctly means 'you decide'.
detection: The first CI run of the suite.
fix: src/chromium_path.js, one shared resolver: the environment variable, then the sandbox directory if it exists, then undefined so Playwright resolves its own.
guard: one shared resolver, so the logic cannot differ between suites
lesson: A path that exists on the machine you wrote the test on is not a path. Resolve environment-specific locations through one helper that falls back to the tool's own default, and return undefined rather than an empty string, because undefined means 'you decide' and an empty string means 'launch nothing'.
cost: one red CI run

title: Twelve profile fields said Saved and never reached the account
symptom: A signed-in user fills in education, intended major, score goal, application year, budget, industry, household income, first generation, military status, study hours or their birth date, sees a Saved toast, and none of it is on their account. It survives only in that browser.
root_cause: Two layers disagreed and nothing compared them. Row Level Security scopes every write on the profiles table to the caller's own row, and a separate column grant decides which columns any role may write at all. The column grant to authenticated covers 5 of the 17 self-reported fields the Account page offers. The page updates the other 12 anyway, the database refuses, and aboutSave wraps the call in a try/catch with an empty body, so the refusal is discarded and the toast fires regardless.
detection: Reading the column privileges while adding new profile fields for something else. Nothing in the product would ever have reported it.
fix: Grant UPDATE on the self-reported columns to authenticated, which is safe because the row policy already restricts every write to the caller's own row, and stop the save path swallowing its own error.
guard: a SQL smoke test asserts authenticated holds UPDATE on every field the Account page writes, and none of the server-owned ones
lesson: An empty catch block around a write is a silent-loss defect waiting to be born. If a save can fail, the person must be told; a success toast that fires regardless of the result is worse than no toast, because it actively teaches the user the data is safe. And where two layers of authorisation have to agree, something has to compare them: the one that is wrong will not announce itself.
cost: every signed-in user's demographics, for as long as the fields have existed

title: The ledger cited commits that squash merging destroys
symptom: CI failed with three assertions at once: six citations unresolvable, the commit count wrong, and the HTML naming the wrong build commit.
root_cause: One cause behind all three. Each incident cites the commit that fixed it, and this repository squash merges, so a branch commit ceases to exist the moment its pull request lands. The builder treated an unresolvable citation as fatal, so it refused to rebuild; build.py catches that failure as a warning rather than stopping the deploy, so the stale committed artefacts stayed on disk and the two freshness assertions then failed against them.
detection: The first CI run after a squash merge, which is the first moment the problem could exist.
fix: Cite the pull request as the durable reference and treat the commit hash as best effort. A citation that no longer resolves is reported and allowed when the record carries a PR number, and is still fatal when it does not.
guard: the builder and smoke_playbook both distinguish a squashed commit from a wrong one
lesson: A commit hash is not a durable citation in a repository that squashes. Pull requests, issues and tags survive history rewriting; branch commits do not. Cite the thing that outlives the merge, and make any check of the other one advisory.
cost: one red CI run, and a document that silently stopped rebuilding

title: The fit card told readers to fill in fields that were below it
symptom: With nothing entered, the comparison card said to fill the three inputs in above, and they are further down the same page.
root_cause: The copy was written while building the card, before deciding where the inputs would live, and was never re-read against the rendered page.
detection: Screenshotting the page and reading it as a user would.
fix: Name the section rather than a direction, and assert the wording in the test so a later move of either block fails loudly.
guard: smoke_fit asserts the card points at the section by name
lesson: Copy that says above, below, left or right is a hard dependency on layout that nothing checks. Name the thing instead, and the sentence survives every rearrangement.
cost: a sentence sending users the wrong way

title: The item counter missed a whole bank file because it assumed a quoting style
symptom: A new bank added 35 items and the build reported the exam's total unchanged at 65. The engine tests, which load the bank for real, saw all 100.
root_cause: The count is a regex over the concatenated source looking for an id in single quotes. The new file emits JSON escaped strings, so its ids are double quoted and none of them matched. Nothing compared the regex count to the number of items that actually load.
detection: Noticing that the build summary and the test output disagreed about the same bank.
fix: Accept either quoting style, and assert that every bank file listed for an exam contributes at least one counted item, so a file the pattern cannot see fails the build instead of counting zero.
guard: per-file contribution assertion in the bank counter
lesson: A regex that counts things assumes a formatting convention, and a file that legitimately breaks the convention counts as zero rather than as an error. Any counter that can return zero for a non-empty input needs a per-source assertion, not just a total.
cost: a published item count 35 short, and a guard that would have kept getting quieter

title: Nothing parsed the one file every user downloads
symptom: None shipped. A bank file with a syntax error built cleanly and the build exited zero, leaving invalid JavaScript in the bank the trainer loads on every visit.
root_cause: The build parses every inline script in every built page, a guard added after an unescaped quote took the whole trainer down at parse time. The item bank is not an inline script. It ships as a separate file and was never in the list, so the largest generated artefact on the site was the one thing the parser never saw.
detection: Deliberately breaking a bank file to test an unrelated guard, and noticing the build passed.
fix: Parse every built bank file and every chunk of it, alongside the pages.
guard: the build node-parses each built bank and chunk
lesson: A parse guard covers the file shapes someone thought of. When the same code moves into a new shape, a separate file, a chunk, a worker, the guard does not follow it. List what the guard covers against what the deploy actually ships, and check the difference rather than the intention.
cost: would have broken every trainer on the next bank edit

title: A repeat metric that gets worse when the bank gets better
symptom: Doubling the LSAT reading bank cut the repeats a student actually sees by 46 percent, from 1875 to 1006, and the bot's avoidable repeats figure went up, from 258 to 309.
root_cause: A repeat counts as avoidable when the student has not yet exhausted that section's pool. Enlarging the pool keeps that condition true for longer in every sitting, so the window in which a repeat is classified avoidable widens with the pool. Measured directly, only 5 of 1300 repeats in a single long run were genuinely avoidable, and both pools were exhausted.
detection: The number moved the wrong way after a change that should only have helped, so the metric was read rather than trusted.
fix: Report the repeat rate per item served alongside the avoidable count, so the student-facing number is visible next to the diagnostic one. The avoidable definition is left alone rather than quietly redefined to make a number look better.
guard: the bot prints repeats per item served next to the avoidable count
lesson: A metric that moves against you when the product improves will eventually be used to justify reverting an improvement. When a number goes the wrong way after a change that should only have helped, measure the underlying thing directly before believing either the number or your own explanation of it. Never redefine the metric in the same change that made it look bad.
cost: nearly a false regression, and a standing hazard for whoever reads it next

title: Correcting a length tell moves it one rank over, every time
symptom: On two separate hand written banks, extending one distractor per item took the longest-is-key rate to near zero and left 25 of 35 and then 30 of 42 keys sitting second longest, so a reader picking the second longest option scored 71 percent on both.
root_cause: Mechanical rather than careless. Extending exactly one distractor past the key moves every key from rank 5 to rank 4 by construction. The recorded ratchet measures only the two extremes, so a corrected bank passes it while carrying a stronger tell one position in.
detection: Measuring the full length rank rather than only the extremes, after the extreme came back clean.
fix: Three passes rather than one, extending a second and third distractor on overlapping subsets, and a shared measure() that prints the whole rank distribution and the best single-rank strategy so the artefact cannot hide behind a passing extreme.
guard: bank_emit.measure prints the full rank and the best single-rank score
lesson: A guard on the extreme of a distribution can be satisfied by moving the mass next to the extreme. When you correct for a measured bias, measure the whole distribution afterwards, not the statistic you were correcting.
cost: two banks that would have passed the ratchet carrying a 71 percent tell

title: The stale count guard checked two nouns and the page used a third
symptom: llms.txt told every model that reads it the LSAT bank holds 65 questions. It held 142. The build's count guard passed the file.
root_cause: The guard matches a number followed by original or flashcards. The LSAT line was phrased as 65 questions today, deliberately, because the number was small and the page said so plainly. The phrasing that made the sentence honest is what put it outside the pattern.
detection: Reading the file while fixing a different count the guard did catch, then watching the widened guard flag a correct sourced figure.
fix: Match a second, unambiguous pattern rather than more nouns. Widening the noun list to items and questions did catch the stale figure, and immediately raised a false positive on '64 questions', which is the real GMAT Focus question count from GMAC and not a bank size at all. A checker that cries wolf gets muted, so the guard now matches 'N original', 'N flashcards' and the specific phrase 'item bank is N', which names our bank and cannot match an exam fact.
guard: the count guard matches original, flashcards, items and questions
lesson: A guard keyed to wording is a guard on the wording, not the fact, and every synonym is a hole in it. Widening the wording is the obvious repair and it trades missed defects for false alarms, which cost more because they get the guard switched off. Match a phrase that only the thing you care about can produce, rather than every word it might happen to use.
cost: a published figure less than half the true one, on the page written for machines

title: The guard against a blind counter was itself blind to three exams
symptom: A new GRE reading bank of 26 items was registered, built, and counted as zero. The published GRE total stayed at 19,888. The guard written a day earlier to catch exactly this said nothing.
root_cause: Two failures of the same shape, one inside the other. The GRE id pattern was G[QVE] and the new ids begin GR, so the counter could not see them. And the per-file guard added for INC-0059, which asserts that every listed bank file contributes at least one counted item, looped over only the two exams that happened to be in hand when it was written.
detection: Predicting it from the id pattern before building, then watching the build confirm it by reporting the old total.
fix: Add R to the GRE pattern, and loop the guard over all five exams rather than two.
guard: the per-file counter guard covers every exam in APPS
lesson: A guard that covers a subset of cases reproduces the original defect in the cases it skips, and it is more dangerous than no guard because the incident it was written for feels closed. When you add a check, enumerate everything of that kind and cover all of it, or state in the code which cases are deliberately excluded and why.
cost: 26 items invisible to every published count, caught before merge
recurs_why: title: the guard against a blind counter was itself blind to three exams

title: The analysis chapter called one file eight failing guards
symptom: The generated chapter reported src/build.py as a guard named by eight incidents, under a heading saying a guard named twice is one that did not hold. build.py contains dozens of unrelated guards and most of those eight are different ones.
root_cause: The recurrence grouping keys on guard_file, which is the file a guard lives in, not the guard. A file that is the natural home for many checks therefore looks like a single check failing repeatedly, and the chapter states that reading in the heading as though it were established.
detection: Reading the generated chapter after a build, to see whether it had picked up a genuine recurrence recorded minutes earlier.
fix: Group by the guard description, which names the mechanism, and report file level clustering separately with wording that says what it actually means.
guard: the analysis chapter groups recurrence by guard rather than by file
lesson: An aggregate is a claim about whatever you grouped by. Group by the file and you have measured the file. State the grouping in the sentence that reports the result, and the overclaim becomes visible while you are writing it.
cost: a generated chapter making a confident and wrong claim about where to spend effort

title: Half the length tell correction did nothing and the build said it had worked
symptom: The new GMAT reading bank corrected its length tell with a table that carries a named number of distractors past the key on each item, so the keys land at spread ranks rather than all at one. The table named 65 items. On 31 of them the authored clause was shorter than the gap it had to close, so the distractor stayed below the key and the item did not move. The run printed an improved distribution and no error, and the 31 were only found by measuring intent against outcome by hand.
root_cause: extend() appends whatever clause the author supplies and checks only that the needle matches exactly one non key choice. Whether the choice ends up longer than the key, which is the entire point of the call, was never checked. The author sizes each clause by eye against a gap reported in a separate run, and an estimate made that way is wrong about half the time.
detection: Comparing the intended lift count for each listed item against the key's actual rank after the run, in a scratch script written because the printed distribution was flatter than before but not as flat as the table should have made it.
fix: check_lift() in bank_emit.py takes the same intent the tables express, one entry per item saying how many distractors were meant to pass the key, and exits naming every item whose key did not land at the matching rank and by how much the clause fell short. The generator calls it after the last extend pass, so a clause that does nothing fails the build instead of being averaged into a number that looks better.
guard: check_lift asserts each lifted item's key rank matches the number of distractors the table lifted
lesson: A correction table is a set of claims about outcomes, and an entry that quietly fails still counts as applied. Aggregate metrics hide this well: a table where half the entries work still moves the number in the right direction, which reads as success. State the per item intent in a form the machine can check, and every entry that did nothing says so by name.

title: The browser path fix covered two suites and three others kept crashing
symptom: smoke_items.js, smoke_consent.js and smoke_billing.js all died at launch with 'Executable doesn't exist at /opt/pw-browsers/chromium_headless_shell-1243/...'. The sandbox holds chromium-1194 and chromium_headless_shell-1194, so Playwright's own resolved path pointed at a build that is not installed. CI passed throughout, because a CI runner installs the browser Playwright expects.
root_cause: INC-0055 was the same failure in smoke_business.js, and the fix was src/chromium_path.js, a shared resolver that prefers CHROMIUM_PATH, falls back to the newest /opt/pw-browsers/chromium-*, and otherwise returns undefined so Playwright decides. Two suites were changed to use it, smoke_business and smoke_fit. The three older suites were left reading process.env.CHROMIUM_PATH directly, which with the variable unset passes executablePath: undefined and hands the decision back to Playwright, which is exactly the case the resolver exists to override. A shared module only helps the callers that call it.
detection: Running the three suites after a bank change, as the pre push checklist requires. They had not been run in this sandbox since the resolver was introduced.
fix: All ten browser suites and playbook_pdf.js now call chromiumPath() from src/chromium_path.js. A check in src/build.py fails the build if any file that launches Playwright does not, and on its first run it named six suites beyond the three the failure had surfaced, plus four more that a grep written from its output then found.
guard: the build refuses a Playwright launch that reads CHROMIUM_PATH instead of calling chromiumPath()
lesson: Extracting a shared helper does not migrate the callers. The extraction fixes the file it was extracted from and leaves every sibling on the old path, which is INC-0059 and INC-0064 in a different costume: a correction applied to the instances in hand rather than to the pattern. Three suites had failed visibly and ten were wrong; the seven silent ones were found by the guard, not by reading. When a helper exists because a direct call was wrong, make the direct call fail the build, and let it enumerate the callers rather than enumerating them by hand.
recurs_why: lesson: which is INC-0059 and INC-0064 in a different costume

title: Shuffling the answers twice put 37 percent of the keys at A
symptom: The new LSAT reading generator printed a key position distribution of 33, 15, 14, 17, 11 across 90 items where an even split is 18 each. Position A held 37 percent of the keys, against a chance rate of 20, which is the exact defect permute() exists to prevent (INC-0039) and which the engine test's answer position check would have failed.
root_cause: The generator called E.permute(I) twice. An intermediate run had ended with permute and measure so the skill counts could be read, and the final block added its own permute before the extend pass, and the earlier pair was never removed. permute seeds a shuffle with crc32 of the item id, so the second call applies the same permutation again, composing it with itself. A permutation composed with itself is not uniform: it favours its own fixed points and short cycles, and with five choices that piles keys onto the position they started at, which is A because items are authored key first.
detection: Reading the generator's own measure output after the length tell was cleared. The length rank line was flat and the key position line on the same screen was not, and it had been on the screen for several runs before it was read.
fix: permute() now stamps each item it has shuffled and exits if it is handed one twice, naming the item. The duplicate call in mk_bank_lsat_rc3.py is removed. The measured distribution after the fix is 20, 19, 19, 16, 16 across 90 items, and the length rank is 18 in every position.
guard: permute refuses to shuffle an item it has already shuffled
lesson: A seeded shuffle is deterministic, which makes calling it twice look harmless: the same input gives the same output. What repeats is the permutation, not the randomisation, and a permutation applied to its own result is biased toward leaving things where they were. Any function whose value comes from being applied exactly once should refuse to be applied twice rather than relying on the caller to remember. The second lesson is about reading: the generator printed the defect on every run, above the line being watched.

title: A bank a student can play at 88 percent, inside a section the check passed
symptom: bank_sat_rw.js ships 32 items on which the longest answer choice is the key 88 percent of the time, and a student who always picks the longest option scores 84 percent on that file against a chance rate of 25. Eighteen other hand written bank files across all five exams carry the same tell at lower strength, several above 50 percent. The engine test reported the SAT Reading and Writing section at 35 percent and passed it.
root_cause: The length bias check groups items by section. A section mixes hand written items with generated ones, and the generated items are flat by construction because the schemas assemble choices mechanically. For SAT Reading and Writing the generated bank supplies 160 of 348 items at 7 percent, which pulls a hand written 88 percent down to a section figure of 35 and under the recorded tolerance of 36. The aggregate was not wrong; it was answering a question nobody needed the answer to. A student does not meet a section, they meet items, and the items arrive from one file at a time.
detection: Measuring the same statistic per source file rather than per section, which was written to find out where the new LSAT and GMAT banks sat relative to the old ones and reported the old ones instead.
fix: The check now runs per hand written source file as well as per section, with its own recorded baseline per file, so a file can only improve. Numeric answer banks are excluded because the separate numeric rank check covers them and character length is the wrong measure for a number. src/bank_repair.py applies an authored clause table to a hand written bank in place, by textual substitution inside the named choice, so the remaining files can be corrected without regenerating a file that was never generated.
guard: length bias is measured per hand written bank file against a recorded baseline, not only per section
lesson: An aggregate over a mixed population reports the population, and if part of that population is flat by construction it will hide the part that is not. The rule that follows is about what the unit of the measurement should be: measure at the grain the defect can exist at, which here is the file, because a file is written by one person in one sitting with one set of habits. The section was the grain the data was convenient at.

title: The second tool that appends a clause did not carry the first one's rule about the full stop
symptom: Two repaired SAT items read 'the number of purchases. made' and 'sleep debt over the course of a week. that they do not fully repay at the weekend'. The clause had been appended after the sentence's own full stop.
root_cause: bank_emit.extend has handled this since it was written: it strips a trailing period, appends the clause and puts the period back. bank_repair.repair was written months later for hand written banks that a generator never produced, and it inserts at the closing quote of the string literal, which is after the period. The rule lived in one implementation rather than in a place both could use, and the second implementation was written from the problem rather than from the first solution.
detection: Reading the per item report after the repair, where the appended text appears at the end of each changed choice.
fix: repair() now inserts before a trailing period, matching extend(). Both behaviours are stated in one comment naming the other function, so the next tool that appends to a choice is written from a rule rather than from scratch.
guard: bank_repair.repair inserts before a trailing full stop, as bank_emit.extend does
lesson: Writing a second tool for the same job in a different context reproduces every detail the first one learned the hard way, unless the detail is written down somewhere the second author will look. This is INC-0067 seen from the other side: there the callers were not migrated to the helper, here the helper's behaviour was not carried into the second implementation. Both are the cost of a rule living in code rather than in a statement of the rule.
recurs_why: lesson: this is INC-0067 seen from the other side

title: Clauses written from a truncated report were appended to the end of the wrong word
symptom: Repaired choices read 'in chronological orderorder', 'return to them afterwardsards', 'how it would spend itintends to spend the money' and 'the bags the proposal would affectl would charge for'. Eleven choices across four bank files were garbled in a way that leaves the file valid JavaScript, leaves the item longer, and moves the measured distribution in the intended direction.
root_cause: The report that shows which distractors need lengthening truncates each choice to fit a terminal line. Several clauses were written as continuations of the truncated text, on the assumption that the tool inserts at the point the needle ends. It does not: repair() appends at the end of the string literal, which is correct for a clause and wrong for a continuation. Nothing distinguished the two, because a continuation is just a clause whose first character is a letter.
detection: Reading the source after a needle failed to match, which showed the previous pass had written 'would spend itintends to spend the money' into the same choice.
fix: repair() refuses a clause that does not begin with a space or punctuation, which is exactly the shape of a continuation. The four affected files were reverted and the repairs redone with clauses written to append rather than to continue.
guard: bank_repair.repair refuses a clause beginning with a letter or digit, which would run into the preceding word
lesson: A report that truncates its output invites the reader to write text that continues it, and a tool that appends will put that text somewhere else. Either the report should not truncate the field the caller has to write against, or the tool should refuse input shaped like a continuation. The cheap half is the refusal, because it is one condition and it cannot be forgotten, while remembering not to write continuations is a habit that has to hold every time.

title: A distractor was replaced and the explanation went on naming the old one
symptom: SR001 offers unremarkable, unaccounted for, unrelated and undisturbed, and its wrong answer note begins 'Unnoticed reverses the point'. Unnoticed is not on the paper. A student reading the explanation after answering is told why an option they were never shown is wrong.
root_cause: The length tell on vocabulary in context items cannot be fixed by appending a clause to a single word, so bank_repair.swap replaces the distractor with a longer one of the same register. It replaces the text in the choices array and nowhere else. An item is not just its choices: expl and wrong name particular options, and on this bank they name them by word.
detection: Reading the item while looking at its shape for a different purpose, three commits after the swap was made.
fix: swap() refuses when the text being replaced appears anywhere else inside the same item, which is exactly where an explanation that names it would be. The one affected note is rewritten to name a distractor that exists.
guard: bank_repair.swap refuses to replace a choice whose text appears elsewhere in the same item
lesson: A record has parts that refer to one another, and a tool that edits one part by text is editing a graph while looking at a string. The cheap guard is not to check every reference but to refuse the edit when the old text occurs anywhere else in the record, because that is the only place a reference to it can be. Refusing on a false positive costs one rewritten table entry; not refusing ships an explanation about an option nobody saw.

title: check_lift was told a one clause entry lifted two distractors
symptom: The GRE reading generator failed with three items named: GR104, GR128 and GR133 were said to have lifted 2 distractors and to belong at rank 3, and each sat at rank 4. Each of the three had exactly one clause in the table.
root_cause: bank_emit.extend accepts a table entry as either one (needle, clause) pair or a list of them, and it is the only place that knows the difference. Every caller of check_lift then has to re-derive the count, and the obvious expression, len(v), reads a bare two element tuple as two lifts. The rule for reading the table lives in extend; the callers each hold a private copy of it, and one copy was wrong.
detection: check_lift failed the generator run and named all three items with their shortfalls.
fix: bank_emit.lift_counts(table) derives the intent from the table using the same tuple or list test extend uses, and every generator that had spelled it out by hand now calls it.
guard: bank_emit.lift_counts is the single reader of the table shape, so check_lift and extend cannot disagree about what an entry says
lesson: A guard that takes the intent as an argument is only as good as the argument, and an argument derived by hand from the same data the guard is checking is a second implementation of the thing being checked. It fails in the direction that is hardest to see: too high an intent demands a rank the clauses cannot reach, and the author satisfies it by writing more clauses than the plan called for, which skews the distribution the other way while every check passes. Derive the intent from the data with the code that already reads it.

title: A corpus field written for one grammatical slot was spliced into another
symptom: 160 of the 833 shipped GMAT v_pc items, 19 percent, offer a choice like "That shorten the time taken to settle a claim is the most urgent of the problems facing Calloway Insurance." It is not English. A student reading it can strike it out without considering the argument, which is a free elimination on a five choice item and makes the item easier than the rating it carries.
root_cause: A PLAN scenario stores goal as a bare infinitive phrase, because the stem it was written for reads "X intends to <goal>". Two other templates splice the same field after "has tried to", where a bare infinitive is also right. One splices it into a subject position, "That <goal> is the most urgent of the problems facing X", where English wants a gerund or a noun phrase. The field is correct; the slot it was reused in is not, and nothing connected the two.
detection: Reading the output of PlanAssume while counting the PLAN corpus in order to widen it. The category had been short since it was written and the shortfall was the reason to look.
fix: Every PLAN scenario gains goal_np, the same goal as a noun phrase, and the subject slot uses it. The bare infinitive stays where a bare infinitive belongs.
guard: framework.verify rejects a stem or choice where That or Whether is followed directly by a bare infinitive, which is what splicing an infinitive goal into a noun slot produces
lesson: A corpus field is written against the one sentence the author had in mind, and the schema that reuses it three templates later has no way to know which shape it is. The type system says str in both places. Two things follow. Store the field in every shape a template needs and name the shapes, rather than storing one shape and trusting the next author to notice. And guard the output, not the corpus: the generated sentence is the only place the mismatch becomes visible, and a cheap pattern over the rendered text catches a class that no check on the inputs can see.

title: Every correct answer on one GMAT schema was ungrammatical, and the guard written an hour earlier could not see it
symptom: All 277 shipped cr_plan_eval items, a third of the GMAT Plan and Construct category, have a key reading "Whether what share of the traffic on Bridge Street stops there at all is what the measure would change." Every one of the eight scenarios produces one, across all six wh words. The student is asked to choose between four fluent distractors and one sentence that is not English, so the item is answerable without reading the argument and is rated as though it were not.
root_cause: The same class as INC-0074 and the same corpus: check is stored as a wh clause because the explanation reads "Establish <check>, and one answer means ...". A second template put it after "Whether" and before "is what the measure would change", where a wh clause cannot go. INC-0074 was the same mistake with the goal field, found in the same reading, and the guard written for it tests for an infinitive after That or Whether. check is not an infinitive, so the guard passed it.
detection: Rendering one item of each plan schema to read the output, immediately after fixing INC-0074 in the schema next to it.
fix: check is rewritten in all scenarios as a clause that reads after "Whether", the trailing "is what the measure would change" is dropped, and the explanation says "Establish whether". The guard is widened from infinitives to any corpus field spliced after That or Whether that does not read as a clause there, and it now runs over the key as well as the distractors.
guard: framework.check_clause_splice refuses a rendered sentence whose That or Whether is followed by a corpus field stored for another slot, tested for every plan field rather than for goal alone
lesson: A guard written from the instance in front of you covers that instance. INC-0074 was a bare infinitive in a noun slot, so the guard looked for bare infinitives, and the sentence one screen away in the same file was a wh clause in a clause slot and went straight through. The general defect was never the infinitive; it was that a corpus field carries no record of the grammatical shape it was written in, and any template may reuse it. So the guard has to be stated over the class, every field against every slot, not over the token that happened to be wrong first. The other half of this is where it was found: the distractor version was spotted first because it is louder, and the version in the key, which is three times as damaging, was found only because the first one prompted a second look. Reading one rendered item per schema would have caught both on the day they were written, and costs less than either fix.
recurs_why: lesson: the guard looked for bare infinitives and the wh clause went straight through

title: str.capitalize() lowercased the rest of the sentence, and took the proper nouns with it
symptom: 180 shipped generated items render a proper noun in lower case. 70 of them carry it in the correct answer: "The fenwick track is the only one in the county, so every competitive runner trains there whether they win or not" and "The halloran fund supplies the starting grant for nearly all of the laboratory's work". The stem two lines above spells both correctly, so the item contradicts itself on the page and the key is the choice that looks wrong.
root_cause: Python's str.capitalize() is not what its name suggests to a reader in a hurry. It uppercases the first character and lower cases every other one. The generators use it twenty one times to render a stored fragment as the start of a sentence, which is right for a fragment of ordinary prose and wrong for any fragment containing a name. Four corpus fields contain one.
detection: Reading one rendered item from each of the five schemas in a category before widening its corpus, which is the practice INC-0075 ended with.
fix: framework.upfirst raises the first character and touches nothing else, and every call site uses it. The four affected fields need no change, which is the point: the fragment was always correct and the renderer was destroying it.
guard: src/build.py fails if str.capitalize() appears anywhere under src/gen, the same way it fails on an em dash
lesson: A standard library function whose name is a plausible description of half of what it does will be used for that half. capitalize() reads as "make this the start of a sentence" and is in fact "make this the start of a sentence and flatten everything else", and the damage is invisible until a value happens to contain a capital. The guard is not a test that the output looks right, because the output looked right for every value that had no name in it. The guard is to ban the function: the correct one is three characters of slicing, the wrong one is never what a generator wants, and a lint catches it in the diff rather than in the bank.

title: A review bot check whose verdict was three coin flips warned on an unrelated bank change
symptom: Widening two GMAT critical reasoning corpora turned the bot's planted weakness check from ok to warn: 2 of 3 sections correctly identified as weakest. Nothing about the diagnosis had changed. The bot threads one seeded generator through every check in an exam, so more items meant the earlier checks consumed a different number of draws and the planted weakness test started from a different point in the stream.
root_cause: The check sat one simulated student per section, three sittings in total, and reported a pass only if all three came out right. Measured over 60 independent seeds the diagnosis is right on 179 of 180 sittings, so at three sittings the check warns on roughly three percent of seeds by sampling alone. Every other check in the bot already averages over 25 sittings; this one did not, and its verdict was therefore a property of the seed as much as of the engine.
detection: The warning appeared on a change that could not plausibly have caused it, so the check was measured across seeds instead of being believed or dismissed.
fix: The check sits five students per section and reports the rate, passing at 90 percent or better and failing below half. The threshold is stated against the measured 99 percent so the margin is visible rather than implied.
guard: the planted weakness check reports a rate over 15 sittings rather than a verdict over 3
lesson: A check that reports pass or fail from a handful of random draws is a check that will flip on work that has nothing to do with it, and the cost is not the false alarm. It is that the next real alarm arrives in a tool people have learned to shrug at. Before believing or dismissing a warning, run the thing it measures enough times to know its rate: that answers both whether this alarm is real and whether the check is worth keeping in its current form. Here the answer was that the engine was fine and the check was wrong, and both were worth knowing.

title: A coefficient of one was printed as 1x on 2,353 shipped items
